factors.desc: Favorable or neutral coverage across the meta's IP archetypes and color strategies. With an expanded 15-deck meta field, decks with fewer polarized matchups perform more reliably across tournament swiss rounds.
Efficient AP usage and energy curve optimization for early and mid-game board development. Includes the ability to deploy threats ahead of curve and maintain proactive pressure.
Maximum damage output potential through Impact, Double Attack, Damage 2, and high BP thresholds. Measures how decisively a deck can close games once its win condition is assembled.
Overall value and composition of triggers in the deck's life area, including Color triggers for resource generation, Active triggers for board impact, and Final triggers for last-resort defense.
Reliable access to key characters and combo pieces through draw, search, and filtering effects. Decks that consistently assemble their core strategy outperform those reliant on natural draws.
Energy and AP economy, hand size management, and long-term card advantage. Measures how efficiently a deck converts its resources into board presence and damage over the course of a game.
Decision tree depth, AP sequencing complexity, and the gap between average and optimal play lines. Decks that reward mastery with significantly higher win rates score well here.
Ability to recover from life damage pressure, board wipes, and resource deficit through trigger activations, defensive keywords, and comeback mechanics.
Adaptable game plans, multi-color tech options, and the ability to pivot between aggressive and defensive postures depending on game state and matchup.

Ability to interfere with the opponent's board state, hand, or game plan through removal, Snipe, retire effects, and denial of key setups. Increasingly relevant as combo-oriented IPs populate the meta.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Erwin Smith / Levi is a midrange deck whose main decisions are when to deploy the Levi bodies, how to meet the energy requirements of the energy line, and which attackers to commit into battles, so it asks for several real choices per turn but not constant branching. Timing matters less, since the deck mostly acts in its own Main Phase with little response play, though the slow curve means a wrong ordering of AP usage can cost tempo. Its strong BP bodies and deep Erwin and Levi pools let a straightforward draw win much of the time, while its slow start and thin disruption make misplays in the early game costly against fast decks.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Compared with the other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, Asta Raid Aggro makes a modest number of real choices each turn, mostly about when to Raid and which character to attack with, and its sequencing is fairly direct. Its matchup dependence is moderate, since its plan is largely the same and only the pacing against CSM or Sakamoto Days changes. Because Raid targets are easy to find and the cheap curve does much of the work, a new pilot keeps much of the deck's win rate, though misjudging a key sideline trade or a race can still cost games.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Kikoru Shinomiya Aggro-Tempo has a moderate number of real decisions per turn, centred on building the energy line early and deciding when to set up Raid turns versus pushing the curve. Its sequencing matters at key moments such as timing the Raid window, but the core plays are fairly readable, so timing is middling. Errors are punished meaningfully because the deck trails faster Sakamoto Days and CSM lists, yet its filtering and cheap bodies soften the cost of a single misstep.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Aki Hayakawa midrange is a mid-complexity Union Arena Standard deck: each Main Phase involves real choices about which characters to play onto the energy line, when to Raid Aki or Himeno, and when to hold removal such as Makima and Fire!, but most turns still follow a clear curve. Its slow start and lack of draw or finishers mean misjudging when to commit or when to pressure costs games, though it is forgiving enough that a competent but not expert pilot keeps much of its win rate, since the four-of core cards do much of the work.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, this Kaoru/Kenshin midrange list has a moderate number of real decisions each turn, mainly around energy-line deployment and when to commit Kenshin threats. Its playsets and cheap Yahiko bodies make its draws fairly predictable, so the autopilot factor sits near the middle, while its awkward curve and weak recovery from a poor opening hand mean a misplay in the early turns is noticeably punished against aggro decks.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard competitive play, this tempo stack is moderately demanding: each turn mixes AP budgeting between events and characters with a few energy-line decisions, but the core Rei opening is largely fixed. Timing matters through the energy line build and BP-battle blocks, yet order is mostly obvious. Matchup play changes some with fast aggro versus slower decks, and misplays of AP spending are costly but often recoverable, while the deck's consistent opening makes it fairly autopilot-friendly.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Shadow Army Raid Midrange asks the pilot to sequence energy-line builds, choose when to deploy Soldiers and Jinwoo, and decide when to raid, which gives a meaningful number of decisions per turn. Its plan shifts sharply against fast aggro versus slower control or big-body lists, so matchup reads matter, while the Soldiers' cheap early bodies and the raid plan make the obvious line fairly forgiving. Missing key pieces in hand is the main way a game is lost, so the pilot's mulligan and early-turn choices carry real weight.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Sinon Aggro-Tempo is a straightforward curve deck with a few meaningful choices per turn: when to commit characters to the energy line, which blocker to remove with Hecate II, and when to spend AP on Photon Sword. Sequencing matters somewhat through energy-line timing but is not as punishing as long interactive chains. The smooth four-of curve lets a competent but not expert pilot win many games, so autopilot is moderately high, while misplaced AP and missed energy lines cost tempo in close games.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, Chainsaw Man is a straightforward aggro-tempo shell: its core plays (Pochita and Denji bodies onto the energy line early, then a strong Chainsaw Man top end) are fairly obvious, so decisions are moderate and mostly about sequencing the 1/2 AP curve and when to commit Chainsaw Man copies. Errors are punished somewhat more than average because the deck lacks disruption and loses races when its early bodies are missing, but its cards do much of the work, keeping autopilot factor above the middle.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, Aoi Todo Boogie Woogie midrange asks for a moderate number of real decisions per turn, especially around when to use Boogie Woogie repositioning and how to sequence the energy line. Its slow curve and lack of burst mean misplays are recoverable but cost tempo in races against faster decks, and Aoi Todo's reliable access makes the deck fairly easy to pilot to a main attacker.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Compared with other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, this midrange list makes a moderate number of decisions per turn, mostly around building the energy line from its Historia bodies, splitting AP across events, and choosing when to commit Levi. Sequencing matters somewhat (Historia and Levi ordering, event timing in the Main Phase), but the Main-Phase-only timing keeps it below the most order-dependent decks. Its low tempo and power mean it relies on the pilot to grind, yet the redundant playsets and simple default lines let a newer player keep much of the deck's win rate.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Evangelion Ragu is a tempo deck whose dense low curve of Proto Type-00 and Rei copies makes early turns fairly straightforward, with decisions concentrated on Raid timing, AP spending and when to commit the mid-game threat. Its limited removal and disruption means it rarely needs complex response timing, but the Sakamoto Days and CSM matchups demand pace-versus-stall reads. Because a strong opening curve wins many games on its own, the autopilot factor is high, though the 11th-place result and blocker-heavy matchups still reward a skilled pilot.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Rimuru Soei Raid Tempo asks for several real decisions a turn: which Gobta or Soei body to Raid with, when to commit energy into the Rimuru lines, and when to swing for damage. Its tempo payoff comes from sequencing Raid correctly, so timing matters more than in a straightforward aggro deck, though its curve and redundancy keep the baseline line fairly obvious. Its 1 AP opening and need for unblocked hits make misplays somewhat punishing, while its strong draw and consistent Rimuru access let it win on autopilot against weaker opposition.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Aki/Denji/Himeno tempo is a fast aggro deck whose turns mostly follow an obvious curve: fill the energy line with four-of characters, then attack wide. Real decisions come from choosing which characters to commit to the line each turn, when to spend AP on Raid upgrades, and whether to hold back against faster boards. Matchup variance is notable because the deck must race Sakamoto Days and Evangelion while being walled by higher-BP blockers. A missed early energy-line character is punished hard, but the four-copy curve gives a new pilot a playable baseline.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Heisuke Mashimo aggro-tempo is a relatively linear deck: a dense, predictable curve of four-of characters lets a pilot curve out with obvious plays, so decisions per turn and sequencing traps sit at a moderate level for competitive Union Arena. Matchup variance is meaningful because the deck is an aggressor that must adjust its plan and attack timing against walls like Solo Leveling and faster racers, while its thin removal and limited reload keep misplays only moderately punishing.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Sakamoto Days aggro-tempo asks for several meaningful choices most turns: which characters to deploy onto the energy line, how to spend AP, and when to commit attackers, with one or two close calls per game. Sequencing matters less than in trigger-heavy decks, but the dense curve of four-of Taro and Shin bodies punishes wasted AP and an awkward hand, and matchups like walls versus races shift the plan noticeably. Much of its win rate comes from the cards themselves, since the board of many bodies pressures opponents with the obvious plays.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard's competitive field, this midrange Kenshin deck asks for steady per-turn choices about AP spending between developing the energy line and committing to raids, with a moderate amount of sequencing around raid timing. Its four-of Kenshin numbers make the obvious raid line fairly reliable, which keeps autopilot relatively high, while misjudging the race against fast Sakamoto Days or Saito builds is costly and matchup planning matters.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Shadow Army Midrange asks for steady decisions each turn: which cheap Soldiers to deploy to the energy line, when to commit AP to Raids, and how to spend energy against a board that is already developing. Its skill ceiling comes mainly from the Sung Jinwoo Raid chain and from hand-ordering to reach the right version, while Soldiers and Arise keep the default line fairly clear. Misplays hurt, especially on setup turns against fast Sakamoto Days lists, but the deck's raw body count is forgiving enough that it is not a razor-thin deck relative to other Standard competitors.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Rimuru Raid Midrange asks for a steady stream of decisions: when to build the energy line toward Raid, which Rimuru version to commit to given split copy counts, and whether to hold removal like Feast or Mystic Thread Strike. The Raid chain's timing and the need to match base characters to Raid cards add sequencing care, while a misplaced base character or slow chain is a moderate rather than fatal error. The deck's raw card power carries much of the win rate, so a competent but not expert pilot still converts many games.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Eva Unit Tempo is a fast, on-curve deck whose turns are mostly straightforward once the energy line is set, so decisions per turn sit mid-range, with the real choices in when to commit threats and which targets to attack. Matchup variance is notable because the deck is weak to the fastest aggro lists and struggles to stall wide boards, so the pilot must adjust its plan. Its power and smooth curve let it win much of the time on autopilot, though the lack of Final-trigger safety and thin removal means a misplay or an early deficit is costly.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Titan Raid Midrange asks for a steady stream of choices each turn: which cheap Titan to deploy, when to commit toward Raid, and whether to spend energy on bodies or Titan Injection. Sequencing matters around the Raid requirement of a named base character, but the timing demands are moderate compared with the most intricate Union Arena decks. A misread on Raid setup or an early stall costs tempo against fast Aggro-Tempo lists, yet the Eren and Zeke payoffs carry enough power that a competent but imperfect pilot can still win many games.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Sakamoto Days is an aggressive tempo deck whose main decisions are how to sequence the cheap energy-line characters, when to commit attackers, and which Taro numbers to run in a given matchup, so it asks for steady decisions rather than deep puzzles. Its mirror games come down to turn order and it falls behind quickly against blockers or faster decks, which makes misplays costly, but its dense low curve and consistent openings let a new pilot win a good share of games with the obvious line.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, this midrange Sword Art Online list is a moderate-difficulty pilot: its few card numbers and four-copy Asuna/Mito curve make turns 1-2 fairly obvious, while decisions about when to commit characters, when to use Photon Sword to win BP battles, and how to pace a game with no finisher add real weight. Its main difficulty comes from matchup-dependent pressure, since Sakamoto Days and Evangelion Tempo punish a slow start, and from having little disruption to answer a snowballing board, which raises the cost of misplays.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Tokyo Ghoul Ayato/Juzo is a midrange deck whose core is a predictable early curve of four-ofs, so most turns have one or two obvious plays and only a few real decisions per game, notably when to commit Juzo or Half-Kakuja. Its sequencing demands are modest for a competitive deck, and the cards do much of the work, though a poor opening hand with no draw or search makes the deck punish mulligan and resource errors somewhat more than its simple line suggests.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, King Engine Midrange sits at a moderate level: each turn offers several real choices about which characters to play, which AP and energy to commit, and what to attack with, but the core King engine line is fairly linear. Sequencing matters at key moments, such as building energy before Saitama, yet it rarely punishes order mistakes harshly thanks to four copies of each King. The deck's high-BP finisher and reliable engine pieces mean a decent draw wins a fair share of games with straightforward play, though close games depend on the pilot's read of the race against fast aggro and the one-plan-fits-most approach.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, Rimuru Raid-chain midrange asks for regular decisions each turn: which Rimuru number to raid into, when to spend AP versus hold energy, and when to fire Mystic Thread Strike. Raid base-matching and the pool of differently-numbered Rimuru create awkward hands that demand careful sequencing, but the deck's core line of dense Soei energy into raided Rimuru is fairly direct. Its mid-tier power and clear strengths mean a competent pilot following the obvious raid chain wins a fair share of games, while misplays around AP tempo against fast decks are moderately costly.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Kenpachi Zaraki is a midrange pile whose turns mostly come down to filling the energy line, then deploying and attacking with big characters, so there are real but not constant choices about what to play and when to attack. Sequencing between the energy line and front line matters, but few plays are order-critical and the stated trigger and removal weaknesses are structural rather than requiring tight timing. Its high-BP bodies win many games on a decent draw, which keeps the autopilot score fairly high, though the clunky hands and slow matchups against aggro decks make matchup reads and mulligan-style decisions important.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this midrange-tempo Suzaku deck sits in the middle of the competitive field: each turn involves several real choices about energy-line buildup, AP spending and when to commit the Lancelot Raid chain, but the early curve is fairly obvious. Its Raid chain requires drawing pieces in the right order, adding some sequencing pressure, while matchup variance is notable because it must shift between racing aggressive life-pressure decks and grinding out a board. Strong early Suzaku draws played the obvious way carry a fair share of games, so autopilot is moderate, while errors in Raid sequencing or pacing against fast decks are often costly.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other Standard Union Arena tournament decks, Yellow Eva is a fairly straightforward midrange-tempo build: duplicated character lines and a mono-color energy base make most turns obvious, with only a few real choices on what to deploy and when to attack. Its main skill demands come from matchup adjustments, such as holding back against fast aggro, and from the tight tempo of its Main Phase sequencing, but a misplay is usually recoverable and a good draw wins on its own.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Ram-led midrange-tempo in Union Arena is a straightforward proactive curve: the energy line is built with cheap Ram copies and most turns have a clear main-phase play, so decision density and sequencing demands sit near the middle of the competitive field. Errors are moderately punished, mainly by missing an early Ram or misusing Demon Power triggers during attacks, while the deck's power and clear plan let a new pilot keep a fair portion of its win rate.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard's competitive field, this Tier 3 aggro-tempo Reze deck makes a moderate number of per-turn choices around curving Denji and Reze plays, with limited sequencing traps since most cards are deployed as drawn. Its plan shifts somewhat between aggressive pressure and defending against top aggro decks, but it is not a deep multi-plan list. Because a good opening hand and the obvious curve win many games, the pilot's influence is real but not dominant.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this Kenpachi Raid aggro-tempo deck has a focused plan: build the energy line with cheap characters, then deploy and Raid with Kenpachi on schedule, so most turns have one or two obvious lines and the deck plays out fairly predictably. Its difficulty comes from AP-cost sequencing on the early 1/2/3 AP turns, the risk of clunky hands with many Kenpachis and little energy, and the need to decide when to commit Bankai or race versus block against faster or midrange opponents.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, this go-wide aggro list makes a moderate number of per-turn decisions around energy-line deployment, AP spending and attack targets, with few response-timing demands since it has almost no disruption or instant-speed interaction. Its cheap 4-of curve lets the pilot play out the obvious plan, so a new pilot keeps much of its win rate, though close games turn on attack and block decisions and misplays in the energy line or BP battles are fairly costly.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Union Arena Zeke Pure Titan is a mid-difficulty midrange deck: each turn involves real choices between developing the energy line (playing cheap Pure Titans at the energy line) and spending AP on Events or the four-copy Zeke top end, but the core line is fairly direct. Sequencing and matchup adjustments matter against aggro versus slower decks, while the tier-3 power and forgiving board presence let a new pilot still win much of the time with the obvious plays.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Compared with other Standard Union Arena tournament decks, Soei Raid Aggro is fairly straightforward: the cheap energy line and four-of Rimuru Raid targets give a clear build-raid-attack plan with few branching choices per turn. Decisions center on timing Raid pieces and holding back when the board is awkward, and misplays such as a wasted Raid window or a poorly timed attack are costly but usually recoverable at this deck's modest ceiling. Its low tier and weak finishers mean most of its win rate comes from its cards, so a new pilot keeps much of the deck's power.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Shuna / Benimaru is a midrange-tempo deck whose early energy-line curve and Raid chains are straightforward to execute, so the pilot makes a handful of meaningful choices per turn (what to deploy, when to Raid, whether to hold Hell Flare) rather than long branching sequences. Timing and ordering of Raids matter moderately, and the plan shifts somewhat between racing aggro decks and holding against midrange or go-wide boards, but a misplay usually costs tempo rather than the game, and a good opening draw plays itself reasonably well.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Purple Ichigo Raid midrange asks for a real choice most turns: which Ichigo or Renji to deploy on the energy line, whether to spend AP on a Raid or on Bankai/Getsugatensho, and which target to remove. Sequencing matters around Raid timing and AP allocation, but it is less punishing than the most intricate Union Arena builds. Its strong Ichigo playsets make the obvious line win a fair share of games, so the pilot's role is significant but not dominant.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Denji aggro-tempo is largely a curve-out deck with a dense, cheap early package, so most turns offer one clear line and the pilot's main decisions are which attacker to commit and when to go for the Bomb Devil burst. Its real skill demands come from matchup-dependent racing against fast Tempo decks and from managing AP and energy lines when the opening stumbles, which raises variance and error costs above a pure autopilot deck.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this Kenshin aggro-tempo deck is built around a dependable opening (a cheap Kenshin starter and an early raid), so a new pilot can make the obvious plays and win a good share of games, giving it a high autopilot score. Decisions are moderate: raid timing, which Kenshin to commit, and when to spend AP each turn matter, but most turns have one clear line. Sequencing and error punishment are middling since AP and energy-line management and raid timing can cost tempo, and matchup variance is moderate because the plan changes mainly between racing and defending against faster aggro decks.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Red Kenshin is a tempo aggro deck whose turns mostly follow a clear pattern: build the energy line early, then Raid onto bodies already on the board, so a typical turn holds a few real choices about what to deploy and attack with, while the Oath Not to Kill and Ryuutsuisen timing add moderate decisions. Sequencing and response-window demands are modest because the deck mostly plays cards in its own Main Phase, but a misplayed opening hand without a cheap energy-line starter or Raid-ready body can stall and lose tempo, and the deck's reliance on one character package makes errors fairly punishing. Its strong, consistent core plan means a competent new pilot keeps much of the deck's win rate.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Cinderella midrange is a mid-difficulty Union Arena deck: each turn asks which characters to play to the energy line and when to commit AP, but the core cards are straightforward and the curve is forgiving, so good draws win with obvious plays. Sequencing matters mainly around the energy line and the Main Phase ordering of characters, with limited response-window decisions since cards mostly act in your own Main Phase. Matchup-dependent choices (fast aggro like REZ and Sakamoto Days versus slower decks) add moderate variance, and a clunky draw of several expensive Cinderella cards can punish misplays in resource allocation.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Crusch & Ferris midrange-tempo sits in the middle of the Standard field: turns involve real choices about which characters to play on the energy line, when to commit to the Crusch Karsten curve, and when to spend events for swing turns, but the redundant four-of core makes most openings fairly obvious. Sequencing matters mainly around the 3-AP turns and event timing in the Main Phase, and misplays are punished moderately given the thin sites and reliance on characters for energy, while a strong draw of Ferris and Karsten still wins a meaningful share of games on its own.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Saito-Kenshin is a tempo aggro deck whose turns mostly follow an obvious curve of deploying characters to the front line and attacking, so decisions per turn are moderate, centered on AP spending and which blockers to push through. Sequencing matters less than in control-leaning Union Arena decks, though energy-line and AP timing still shape early turns. Its cheap curve and playsets let a fresh pilot keep much of the deck's win rate, but close races against fast aggro and midrange boards are decided by careful pilot choices.

skillRating.label: Advanced
skillRating.reasoning: Titan Raid Midrange asks the pilot to choose each turn among raid targets, AP spending under the 3-AP cap, when to commit characters, and which battles to take, giving it real per-turn decisions. Sequencing matters for chaining Raids and keeping the energy line going, and a lost battle or sideline can wipe out a turn's investment. The deck's raw power and the obvious Raid ladder let a new pilot win many games on autopilot, while close games turn on matchup reads against fast Aggro-Tempo decks.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other competitive Standard Union Arena decks, this Eren Raid midrange list asks for a steady stream of attack, Raid and energy-line decisions each turn, with a moderate amount of sequencing around when to Raid onto a base character. Matchup handling matters against fast aggro, and Raid's dependence on the right base character makes misplays moderately costly, though the strong Eren threats let the cards carry much of the win rate.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
